title: Constant-extension Weil hearts, cyclic sheets and residue-degree Frobenius powers
statement:
Fix the finite-field datum $(p,a,q,k_0,k)$ of [def-weil-finite-field-fiber], a prime $\ell\ne p$, an algebraic closure $\Qlb$ of $\mathbf Q_\ell$, and $\iota:\Qlb\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbf C$ as in [def-weil-punctual-weights]. Let $X_0$ be a separated finite-type $k_0$-scheme, $X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$, $m\ge1$, $k_m=\mathbf F_{q^m}\subset k$, $X_{0,m}=X_0\times_{k_0}k_m$, and $g_m:X_{0,m}\to X_0$ the projection. All coefficient categories and constructible Weil sheaves are those of [def-weil-weil-sheaf-complex] and [def-weil-constructible-heart].

(a) For any constructible Weil sheaf $\mathcal F=(M,\theta)$ on $X_0$, its restriction to the $k_m$-scheme $X_{0,m}$ has underlying object $M$ on $X$ and Weil map
$$\theta^{[m]}=\theta\circ Lg_X^*\theta\circ\cdots\circ L(g_X^{m-1})^*\theta,$$
where $g_X$ is geometric Frobenius [def-weil-frobenius-detailed]. This restriction is exact. If $z\in X_{0,m}$ is closed with image $x\in X_0$ and $f=[\kappa(z):\kappa(x)]$, its local operator, using exactly the iterated point transports of [def-weil-local-frobenius-trace], is conjugate to $F_x^f$, and $q_z=q_x^f$. Equivalently, if $d=[\kappa(x):k_0]$, then $f=m/\gcd(d,m)$. These assertions hold for constructible sheaves, without a lissity or semisimplicity hypothesis.

(b) Write $W_{k_m}(X_{0,m})$ for its constructible Weil heart as a $k_m$-scheme and $W_{k_0}(X_{0,m})$ for its constructible Weil heart when the same scheme is viewed over $k_0$. The geometric scheme in the second category is $X_{0,m}\times_{k_0}k$, a disjoint union of $m$ sheets isomorphic to $X$, cyclically permuted by geometric $q$-Frobenius. Restriction to the sheet for the inclusion $k_m\subset k$, together with the return isomorphism around this cycle, gives an exact equivalence
$$W_{k_0}(X_{0,m})\simeq W_{k_m}(X_{0,m}).$$
Its inverse places the successive Frobenius translates on the sheets and uses the given $q^m$-Weil map for the return. It identifies subobjects, quotients and finite filtrations. At a closed point $z$ of $X_{0,m}$ the two interpretations have the same local operator up to conjugacy and the same absolute residue size $\#\kappa(z)$. Thus corresponding quotients are punctually pure of the same weight, and finite mixed filtrations with any specified weight bound correspond. Applied to the object in (a), the inverse gives precisely the $k_0$-Weil pullback $g_m^*\mathcal F$ on this disjoint geometric scheme, before applying $g_{m,*}$.

source.place: Paragraphs 1 and 5: constant-extension local operators and the cyclic-sheet identification before finite direct image; definition-level point transports, with residue degree f rather than extension degree m.

proof.text: Put $Y=X_{0,m}\times_{k_0}k$ and $H=\operatorname{id}_{X_{0,m}}\times\operatorname{Spec}(\gamma)$. The extension $k_m/k_0$ is Galois with cyclic Frobenius group of order $m$. Apply the finite Galois tensor decomposition with $E=k_m$, $L=k_0$, and then extend its first factor from $k_m$ to $k$. It gives $k_m\otimes_{k_0}k\simeq\prod_{\sigma:k_m\hookrightarrow k}k$. Base changing $X_0$ therefore decomposes $Y$ into $m$ open-and-closed sheets. Let $j_0:X\to Y$ denote the inclusion corresponding to $k_m\subset k$, and put $h_i=H^i j_0$ for $0\leq i<m$. Frobenius acts transitively on the embeddings, so these are precisely the sheets. Directly on tensor coordinates, $H^m j_0=j_0 g_X^m$. The latter map is geometric Frobenius for the $k_m$-model. The maps $h_i$ are isomorphisms onto their sheets as schemes; for $i>0$ they need not be $k$-linear.

source.place: (1.1.7), pp.150–151; paragraph following (1.1.10), p.152: change of finite base field and geometric disjoint union

proof.text: Restriction to the sheets decomposes the bounded constructible categories and their cohomology componentwise, including at $\Qlb$ coefficients, by the finite-clopen decomposition. Pullback by each sheet isomorphism and its inverse is an exact inverse-image equivalence at finite and integral coefficients. Its derived pullback is that inverse image. Rationalization extends these functors and their inverse identities, and the common-stage construction extends them to $\Qlb$. Consequently these identifications preserve the standard heart and its kernels and cokernels. This applies also to the semilinear automorphism $g_X$; write $P=Lg_X^*$ on the heart. Thus $P$ and every $h_i^*$ used below are exact equivalences. No assertion of $k$-linearity of $h_i$ is needed.

source.place: Tag 04TS, sites-lemma-mapping-property-glue; coefficient and derived enhancements are the cited finite-clopen and isomorphism-pullback statements

proof.text: For $(N,\eta)$ in $W_{k_0}(X_{0,m})$, set $A_i=h_i^*N$. The canonical pullback-composition comparisons and step 1 identify its Weil map with arrows $a_i:A_{i+1}\xrightarrow{\sim}A_i$ for $i<m-1$ and $a_{m-1}:P^m A_0\xrightarrow{\sim}A_{m-1}$. Send this tuple to $(A_0,\phi)$, where $\phi=a_0\circ\cdots\circ a_{m-1}:P^m A_0\xrightarrow{\sim}A_0$; on morphisms use the component on sheet zero. This is a $k_m$-Weil sheaf because its geometric Frobenius is $g_X^m$. Conversely, from $(A,\phi)$ form the tuple $A_i=A$, $a_i=\operatorname{id}$ for $i<m-1$, $a_{m-1}=\phi$, and glue it by the inverse of the clopen equivalence in step 2. On the actual sheets these are the successive Frobenius translates of $A$. A morphism $u$ commuting with the return map gives the componentwise morphism $u_i=u$ of these tuples, including the last arrow by $u\phi=\phi'P^m(u)$. This defines the inverse functor explicitly.

source.place: p.152, paragraph following (1.1.10): invariance of Weil sheaves under changing the finite base field, expanded into transition arrows

proof.text: The return functor followed by this construction is the identity on $(A,\phi)$. For an arbitrary cyclic tuple, define $r_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $r_i=a_0\circ\cdots\circ a_{i-1}:A_i\xrightarrow{\sim}A_0$ for $1\leq i<m$. These give an isomorphism from the tuple to the normalized tuple of its return: $r_i a_i=r_{i+1}$ for $i<m-1$, while $r_{m-1}a_{m-1}=\phi P^m(r_0)$. If $u_i$ is a morphism of tuples, its commuting squares imply $r_i' u_i=u_0 r_i$ by induction on $i$, proving naturality. Hence the two functors are quasi-inverse. For $m=1$ there are no intermediate arrows and both functors are the identity.

source.place: p.152, change-of-base-field paragraph: explicit unit, counit and naturality calculation

proof.text: The underlying constructible hearts are abelian. Because $P$ is exact, kernels and cokernels of commuting Weil morphisms inherit invertible Weil maps: apply $P$ to the kernel (respectively cokernel) universal diagram and use the two original invertible structure maps to identify its universal object. Their universal properties then hold in the category of pairs, since the underlying factorization is unique and the commuting equation follows after composing with the kernel inclusion or cokernel projection. Thus exactness of a Weil sequence is detected on its underlying sheaves. The restriction and normalized inverse above are componentwise exact by step 2, so the equivalence is exact. It carries monomorphisms, their quotients, and finite chains to the corresponding ones; using the inverse gives all subobjects and filtrations in either direction.

source.place: Paragraphs 1 and 5: constant-field restriction and descent; explicit cyclic-sheet calculation

proof.text: Let $z$ be a closed point of $X_{0,m}$, and put $r=[\kappa(z):k_m]$. Its residue field is finite and has cardinality $q^{mr}$. For the $k_0$-interpretation the local operator uses $mr$ transitions of $H$; for the $k_m$-interpretation it uses $r$ return transitions of $H^m$. Expanding the latter return maps gives exactly the same $mr$ factors of $\eta$, in the same order. The point transports also agree: finite-level composition identifies the transport for $\gamma^m$ with the block of $m$ transports for $\gamma$; the whole-tower power identity and its specified integral realization give this identity before rationalization, rather than merely after separate reductions. Rationalizing preserves the equality, and naturality and coefficient compatibility give it on the common-stage $\Qlb$ category. Repeating $r$ blocks therefore gives precisely the point transport used in the $k_0$ local operator. On the chosen sheet the two operators are equal under the canonical stalk identification; another choice conjugates this identification. This proves the local-operator assertion in (b), with the same absolute residue size $q^{mr}$ in both interpretations.

source.place: (1.1.7)–(1.1.10), pp.150–152; compatibility with the specified point transports is supplied by the cited composition and whole-tower identities

proof.text: Define restriction in (a) by $(M,\theta)\mapsto(M,\theta^{[m]})$. Pullback composition identifies $L(g_X^m)^*$ with $P^m$. Multiplying the $m$ pullbacks of the commuting equation for a morphism proves that it commutes with $\theta^{[m]}$, so this is a functor; it is exact because its underlying functor is the identity and exactness is detected there by step 5. Let $\pi:Y\to X$ be the geometric base change of $g_m$. It satisfies $\pi H=g_X\pi$ and $\pi j_0=\operatorname{id}_X$. Hence the restriction of $\pi^*(M,\theta)$ to sheet zero is $M$, and the product of its $m$ Weil transitions is exactly $\theta^{[m]}$, by composing the pullbacks of $\theta$. The equivalence of (b) therefore sends $g_m^*\mathcal F$ to this restriction. Its inverse recovers $g_m^*\mathcal F$ canonically up to the natural isomorphism of step 4; this assertion is made before any direct image.

proof.text:
Apply the constructible Weil pullback/local-Frobenius theorem to the $k_0$-morphism $g_m:X_{0,m}\to X_0$. Its source is separated and of finite type over $k_0$, since $k_m/k_0$ is finite. For $x=g_m(z)$, that theorem gives the compatible-stalk identity $F_{z,g_m^*\mathcal F}=F_x^f$ up to conjugacy, and $q_z=q_x^f$, where $f=[\kappa(z):\kappa(x)]$. Steps 6–7 identify its left side with the local operator of the restriction in (a), proving the required assertion without lissity or semisimplicity.
For the stated formula, write $d=[\kappa(x):k_0]$ and $R=[\kappa(z):k_0]$. The finite field $\kappa(z)$ is the quotient of $\kappa(x)\otimes_{k_0}k_m$ by the prime specifying $z$, and is generated by the images of its two factors. Thus $d\mid R$ and $m\mid R$. Its $q$-power automorphism has order $R$. The power $\operatorname{lcm}(d,m)$ fixes both generating fields, so is the identity; hence $R\mid\operatorname{lcm}(d,m)$. Conversely the two divisibilities imply $\operatorname{lcm}(d,m)\mid R$, giving $R=\operatorname{lcm}(d,m)$. Therefore $f=R/d=m/\gcd(d,m)$.

source.place: (1.1.8), p.151: Frobenius raised to the residue extension degree; finite-field degree computation spelled out

proof.text: For corresponding subquotients under (b), step 6 identifies the local eigenvalues up to conjugacy at every closed point, and leaves $q_z=\#\kappa(z)$ unchanged. Thus the equations $|\iota(\alpha)|=q_z^{w/2}$ agree for every real $w$. Exactness identifies the successive quotients of any finite filtration, so purity of each quotient, its weight and any specified upper weight bound agree. Applying the inverse functor proves the converse. The argument includes zero stalks (whose purity condition is vacuous), zero objects and the empty scheme.
